t: Why You Should Respond Slowly To Misbehavior https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/06/30/why-you-should-respond-slowly-to-misbehavior/
q: There is a compulsion among teachers to react too quickly to misbehavior. As soon as it shows up on their radar, they’re on it in a flash, making judgments and decisions before fully understanding what it is.
But rushing toward the first suspicion of misbehavior or calling out in an attempt to interrupt it is like trying to stop milk as it’s being spilled. Once a rule has been broken, it’s broken.

It’s tough to keep your cool when you’re rushing to handle misbehavior. The stress and tension of thinking and moving fast on your feet can cause you to raise your voice or say something you’ll regret.
Dealing with misbehavior too quickly risks inciting students who are already in a heightened state, which all but guarantees an argumentative response.
Effective classroom management demands that you get the facts first before responding to misbehavior. Teachers who are quick to react often get it wrong, causing students to distrust them intensely.
By merely responding methodically to misbehavior, you’ll empower yourself to keep your composure, maintain control of your class, and make the right decisions with grace, clarity, and conviction.

t: How To Use The Preview Strategy To Improve Behavior e-behavior/
q: The preview strategy is intrinsic in nature and involves a simple piquing of your students’ interest in the activities you have planned for the day.

When you’re looking over your lesson plans before school, or better yet, when you’re first creating them, search for that “one thing” in each lesson that is potentially most interesting to your students.
The most effective teachers are able to provide for their students compelling reasons why they should pay attention, why they should lean forward and care about what they’re about to learn.
Unless you have a learning environment your students enjoy and look forward to coming to every day, then there isn’t a rule or consequence in the world that is likely to help.
So look for that “one thing” in every lesson. Reignite the joy of learning for your students.
One of the great things about the preview strategy is that it will cause you to really sell what you’re teaching.

t: How To Be Consistent With Classroom Management gement/
q: The solution is confidence, confidence in knowing that it is indeed best to follow through with your classroom management plan every single time.
To enforce your agreed-upon consequences sometimes and not others is grossly unfair to your students.
Whenever you say you’re going to do something and don’t do it, you lose a layer of respect from your students.
When your most challenging students learn that you’re not so committed to enforcing consequences, that your classroom management plan is written in pencil, they’ll smell blood in the water.
Wherever there is weak accountability or semi accountability, behavior, respect, and kindness take a nosedive.

A well-written classroom management plan, on the other hand, followed as taught, modeled, and practiced, is fair to all students and never creates resentment, friction, and hard feelings between the teacher and her students.

t: Why Before School Is The Perfect Time To Build Rapport https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/06/09/building-rapport-with-students-before-school/
q: Because having rapport with students translates to powerful and behavior-influencing leverage—the kind of leverage that compels them to want to behave, to want to do well, and to want to please you.
Simply being with your students outside the limits of the classroom is an easy, organic way to build rapport.
The idea that yesterday’s mistakes and misbehaviors are forgotten is an important part of an overall strategy to turn around your most difficult students.
The biggest mistake teachers make when attempting to build rapport is that they try too hard. They dominate the conversation—talking at, rather than with, students.
The truth is, having a healthy, trusting, and influential rapport with students, the kind that gives your classroom management plan relevance and meaning, is primarily a function of your likeability.
Listen more than talk. Don’t try so hard. Let the conversation come to you—and then let it go where it goes.

t: Are You Sabotaging Your Own Classroom Management Success? ement-success/
q: The fact is, it doesn’t matter where you teach or who shows up on your roster, the well-behaved classroom you long for is within your grasp.
A defeatist point of view will undermine everything you do—sealing your fate to a career of frustration, disappointment, and dissatisfaction.
In order to create the class you really want, you have to believe deep down that you can—not merely as a possibility, but as a foregone conclusion that you will.
The truth is, offering excuses, even in the privacy of your own mind, is akin to giving up on your students—as well as on yourself.
By taking responsibility for everything within the four walls of your classroom, you instantly become a better, more effective teacher.
There are scores of teachers all over the world, some in the most difficult circumstances imaginable, who this very minute are enjoying the dream class they’ve always wanted.
